I checked on the [arithmetic with units](https://docs.sunpy.org/en/stable/tutorial/units.html#arithmetic-with-units) operation. It turns out that there can't be an explicit conversion to a `int` from a default `floating point` when operating on values.
Here's a test case:
```
distance_start = 10 * u.mm
distance_end = 23 * u.km
displacement = distance_end - distance_start
displacement

time = 15 * u.minute
speed = displacement / time               
int(displacement / time)
speed
```

On testing the code, it returns the value `1.5333327 km/min`. This is a float value. I want it to covert it to an integer. It can't be done presently.
When I type, say this:
```
import math
print(math.floor(speed))
```

Following error finds the way:
```
UnitConversionError                       Traceback (most recent call last)
[/usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/astropy/units/quantity.py](https://localhost:8080/#) in to_value(self, unit, equivalencies)
    986             try:
--> 987                 scale = self.unit._to(unit)
    988             except Exception:

9 frames
[/usr/local/lib/python3.10/dist-packages/astropy/units/core.py](https://localhost:8080/#) in _to(self, other)
   1191 
-> 1192         raise UnitConversionError(f"'{self!r}' is not a scaled version of '{other!r}'")
   1193 

UnitConversionError: 'Unit("km / min")' is not a scaled version of 'Unit(dimensionless)'
```


Or if I try to explicitly convert it, say through this:
`speed = int(displacement / time)`
or 
`speed = displacement // time`

It returns:
`UnitDimensionError`

It would be really helpful for a new feature to be added here

### Proposed solution

Now I understand Dimensionality is an important feature aspect here, especially when errors can be made when converting the units.
One way is by first calculating the scalars and then adding the dimensions to the units. Say in the above example, first I calculate the scalar values of `displacement/time`, then concatenate their dimensions to the value.

- A `HelioprojectiveRadial` coordinate frame
- A `make_hpr_header()` header helper
- A `show_hpr_impact_angle()` ~context manager~ function to modify a WCSAxes axis to show impact angle

- A `make_hpr_header()` header helper
- A `show_hpr_impact_angle()` ~context manager~ function to modify a WCSAxes axis to show impact angle

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/78eed27e-60ba-43ba-8253-9108e05967b5)

I get the following results:

```
*******************************************************************************
 Date__(UT)__HR:MN     R.A._____(ICRF)_____DEC  R.A.__(a-apparent)__DEC
***********************************************************************
 2024-Nov-01 00:00     14 25 20.09 -14 24 19.7  14 26 39.85 -14 30 57.7
```

For the record here is the geodetic position of the observer as reported by Horizons:

```
Center geodetic : 359.8833, 51.5, 9.9807E-13      {E-lon(deg),Lat(deg),Alt(km)}
```

If I now try and do the same with astropy, I get:

```python
In [1]: from astropy.time import Time
   ...: from astropy import units as u
   ...: from astropy.coordinates import EarthLocation, get_body

In [2]: 
   ...: london = EarthLocation.from_geodetic(359.8833 * u.deg, 51.5 * u.deg)
   ...: time = Time("2024-11-01T00:00:00")

In [3]: coord = get_body("sun", time=time, location=london, ephemeris="jpl")
   ...: print(coord.to_string("hmsdms"))
14h25m18.72847303s -14d24m13.08322263s
```

This is close to although not quite the same as the Horizons Astrometric RA/Dec, but quite a bit offset from the Horizons Apparent RA/Dec. What is confusing however is that the docstring for ``get_body`` says that it should be returning apparent coordinates.

your Astropy code is essentially printing the "apparent" RA/dec oriented to ICRF.  "Apparent" here means that it is correcting for light travel time (via `get_body()`) and for stellar aberration (via `GCRS`).  It is possible – with some effort – to reconstruct the astrometric RA/dec oriented to ICRF for comparison to Horizons, but as you have already seen in #10230, that functionality is not readily available.  For ground observers, the difference between astrometric and apparent RA/dec should be no more than tens of arcseconds.

Second, the "apparent" RA/dec reported by Horizons is _not_ oriented to ICRF.  Here's their definition:
```
 'R.A.__(a-apparent)__DEC' =
  Airless apparent right ascension and declination of the target center
with respect to an instantaneous reference frame defined by the Earth equator
of-date (z-axis) and meridian containing the Earth equinox of-date (x-axis,
EOP-corrected IAU76/80). Compensated for down-leg light-time delay,
gravitational deflection of light, stellar aberration, precession & nutation.
Note: equinox (RA origin) is offset -53 mas from the of-date frame defined
by the IAU06/00a P & N system.
```
That is, we need to compare using a frame other than `GCRS` because we need to include precession and nutation (and technically gravitational deflection of light).  The closest Astropy frame is `PrecessedGeocentric`, which does go beyond `GCRS` in including precession, but there's no native frame that additionally includes nutation.  Extending your example:
```python
In [4]: coord.equinox = time  # Set this frame attribute on SkyCoord to create the equinox-of-date PrecessedGeocentric frame
   ...: print(coord.precessedgeocentric.to_string("hmsdms"))
14h26m40.18189722s -14d30m53.14327595s
```
Note that this is now very close to the Horizons values(`14 26 39.85 -14 30 57.7`), even though nutation is not included in the Astropy values.

As an aside, I'll mention that you're using the default JPL ephemeris for `astropy`, which is DE430, but Horizons is using a newer one.  xref #11609","reactions":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/astropy/astropy/issues/comments/2451884947/reactions","total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"hooray":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"performed_via_github_app":null}}

am trying to use ``get_body`` to get the RA/Dec for the sun on a certain date, and am interested in getting the apparent coordinates consistent with JPL horizons. If I go to [Horizons](https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/app.html#/) and choose the following settings:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/78eed27e-60ba-43ba-8253-9108e05967b5)

I get the following results:

```
*******************************************************************************
 Date__(UT)__HR:MN     R.A._____(ICRF)_____DEC  R.A.__(a-apparent)__DEC
***********************************************************************
 2024-Nov-01 00:00     14 25 20.09 -14 24 19.7  14 26 39.85 -14 30 57.7
```

For the record here is the geodetic position of the observer as reported by Horizons:

```
Center geodetic : 359.8833, 51.5, 9.9807E-13      {E-lon(deg),Lat(deg),Alt(km)}
```

If I now try and do the same with astropy, I get:

```python
In [1]: from astropy.time import Time
   ...: from astropy import units as u
   ...: from astropy.coordinates import EarthLocation, get_body

In [2]: 
   ...: london = EarthLocation.from_geodetic(359.8833 * u.deg, 51.5 * u.deg)
   ...: time = Time("2024-11-01T00:00:00")

In [3]: coord = get_body("sun", time=time, location=london, ephemeris="jpl")
   ...: print(coord.to_string("hmsdms"))
14h25m18.72847303s -14d24m13.08322263s
```

This is close to although not quite the same as the Horizons Astrometric RA/Dec, but quite a bit offset from the Horizons Apparent RA/Dec. What is confusing however is that the docstring for ``get_body`` says that it should be returning apparent coordinates.

If this is user error, it would be nevertheless helpful to indicate in the ``get_body`` docstring how to get results consistent with JPL Horizons since this will be a common use case, and it would also be helpful to know how to select between astrometric versus apparent Description

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox_(celestial_coordinates)

Wikipedia page says that J2000 should be defined in UTC as January 1st, 2000 at 11:58:55. However it is returned in astropy as a datetime object holding January 1st 2000, at 12:00:00 UTC. Leading to a discrepancy of over a minute. 


https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leap_second

In addition, I'm pretty sure that 5 extra leap seconds are being added to datetime objects when converting astropy Times to datetime objects. Only 27 leap seconds should be added to UTC. Likely this difference arises because TT is 32 seconds ahead of TAI. While UTC is 37 seconds ahead of TAI. While I'm not familiar with all of astropy's code, I get this idea because the CDFEpoch library: https://cdflib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/cdflib.epochs.CDFepoch.html; defines a variable J2000LeapSeconds= 32.0. However, CDFEpoch also offers to use astropy internally for the conversion, and I'm guessing their implementation was designed to match astropy's as they offer both: https://cdflib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/cdflib.epochs_astropy.CDFAstropy.html#cdflib.epochs_astropy.CDFAstropy


### Expected behavior

Datetime objects in python are to hold UTC times by default, users will expect the times to be in UTC; NOT Terrestrial Time

### How to Reproduce

```python
import astropy
import astropy.time

t = astropy.time.Time(2451545.0, format="jd", scale="utc")

print(t.datetime)
```

```
2000-01-01 12:00:00
```

Notice that it says January 1st, 2000 at 12:00:00 rather than January 1st, 2000 at 11:58:55. Also notice that autoplot disagrees with astropy by 1 minute and 9 seconds when converting a CDF_TT2000 epoch to UTC. Likely this is because the autoplot team is defining J2000 correctly and only adding 27 leap seconds to UTC for the present date rather than 32.

So, the correct code is:
```python
>>> t = astropy.time.Time(2451545.0, format="jd", scale="tt")
>>> print(t.utc.datetime)
2000-01-01 11:58:55.816000
```
Note that you also have to explicitly convert the time to UTC (`t.utc`) before converting it to a `datetime.datetime` instance.

Instead of typing out the JD, you can alternatively simply use the `"J2000"` shorthand:
```python
>>> t = astropy.time.Time("J2000", scale="tt")
>>> print(t.utc.datetime)
2000-01-01 11:58:55.816000
```
I stress again that if you want to create a `Time` instance for the J2000.0 epoch, you need to explicitly specify `scale="tt"`.

Regarding leapseconds, you'll have to share some code or reference for why you think Astropy is incorrect. I am trying to do the transfomation from ITRS to topocentric AltAz frame using SkyCoord.transform_to() functionality:
altazCoord = itrsCoord.transform_to(AltAz(obstime=time, location=obsGeoLocation)

The problem encountered is that under Astropy version 4.0 we are receiving different values than under Astropy version 5.3.1. Based on external validator we know that the values from version 4.0 are correct. I assume that some correction or some parts of the transformation was omitted in version 5.3.1 or replaced by other function. Can somebody suggest, what should be added to have equal values under astropy 5.3.1 in comparison to version 4.0?

Example outputs:

Current values - Astropy version 5.3.1
<SkyCoord (AltAz: obstime=60573.003523216925, location=(4053731.93746628, 1260550.54234471, 4744894.08614764) m, pressure=0.0 hPa, temperature=0.0 deg_C, relative_humidity=0.0, obswl=1.0 micron): (az, alt, distance) in (deg, deg, m)

    (169.68410928, 67.35684178, 23624155.6380583)>

### How to Reproduce

# run the bellow code snippet with astropy versions 4.0 and 5.3.1 or the latest. The results will differ, and the 4.0 version is only giving the real values.

from astropy.coordinates import EarthLocation, SkyCoord, AltAz
from astropy.time import Time
import astropy.units as u

time = Time(60573.003523216925, format='mjd', scale='utc')

itrsCoord = SkyCoord(x=23787247.15570922, y=9102499.0451817, z=15098296.92876073, unit='m',
                     representation_type='cartesian', frame='itrs', obstime=time)

obsGeoLocation = EarthLocation(lat=48.372528 * u.deg, lon=17.2736306 * u.deg, height=536.1 * u.m)

altazCoord = itrsCoord.transform_to(AltAz(obstime=time, location=obsGeoLocation))

```python
from astropy.coordinates import EarthLocation, SkyCoord, AltAz
from astropy.time import Time
import astropy.units as u

time = Time(60573.003523216925, format='mjd', scale='utc')

obsGeoLocation = EarthLocation(lat=48.372528 * u.deg, lon=17.2736306 * u.deg, height=536.1 * u.m)

itrsCoord = SkyCoord(x=23787247.15570922 * u.m - obsGeoLocation.x,
                     y=9102499.0451817 * u.m - obsGeoLocation.y,
                     z=15098296.92876073 * u.m - obsGeoLocation.z,
                     location=obsGeoLocation,
                     representation_type='cartesian', frame='itrs', obstime=time)

altazCoord = itrsCoord.transform_to(AltAz(obstime=time, location=obsGeoLocation))

print(altazCoord)
```

## PR Description

This is a vectorized rewrite of the attempt in #6885.

For interpolation methods other than `astropy` and `nearest`, the end-points of the arc along which to sample may not be included in the interpolation. So, it is often better to add the 4 nearest neighbors to the simplices found by `smap.wcs.world_to_array_index` (which uses `astropy.wcs.WCS.all_world2pix`). See below (hollow markers are grid points; red grid points are used for interpolation; blue markers are the arc along which to interpolate):

![plot_neighbor_finder](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/72d78d84-7322-42c5-9207-94e91640d2c9)

Also, here is a comparison of all supported interpolation methods.

![compare_methods](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ce844dca-03d4-4ccf-8251-228fd9f15493)

`astropy` and `nearest` agrees exactly, as expected. But there can be quite large differences in the other interpolation methods. ## PR Description

This is a vectorized rewrite of the attempt in #6885.

For interpolation methods other than `astropy` and `nearest`, the end-points of the arc along which to sample may not be included in the interpolation. So, it is often better to add the 4 nearest neighbors to the simplices found by `smap.wcs.world_to_array_index` (which uses `astropy.wcs.WCS.all_world2pix`). See below (hollow markers are grid points; red grid points are used for interpolation; blue markers are the arc along which to interpolate):

![plot_neighbor_finder](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/72d78d84-7322-42c5-9207-94e91640d2c9)

Also, here is a comparison of all supported interpolation methods.

![compare_methods](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ce844dca-03d4-4ccf-8251-228fd9f15493)

`astropy` and `nearest` agrees exactly, as expected. But there can be quite large differences in the other interpolation methods. +    Examples

+
+    >>> # Right neighbors
+    >>> get_neighboring_indices(indices, [1, 0], [5, 5])
+    array([[1, 2, 3, 4],

+
+    >>> # Left neighbors

+    array([[0, 1, 2, 3],

+    array([[1, 2, 3, 4],

+
+    """

+        & (y <= dimensions[1] - 1)

## PR Description

This is a vectorized rewrite of the attempt in #6885.

For interpolation methods other than `astropy` and `nearest`, the end-points of the arc along which to sample may not be included in the interpolation. So, it is often better to add the 4 nearest neighbors to the simplices found by `smap.wcs.world_to_array_index` (which uses `astropy.wcs.WCS.all_world2pix`). See below (hollow markers are grid points; red grid points are used for interpolation; blue markers are the arc along which to interpolate):

Also, here is a comparison of all supported interpolation methods.

![compare_methods](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ce844dca-03d4-4ccf-8251-228fd9f15493)

`astropy` and `nearest` agrees exactly, as expected. But there can be quite large differences in the other interpolation methods. import numpy as np
from astropy.stats import sigma_clip
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
import scipy.sparse as sp
from astropy.io import fits
from tqdm import trange
from astropy.wcs import WCS
from spectral_cube import SpectralCube as sc
import astropy.units as u

np.seterr(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore")
np.set_printoptions(precision=12, suppress=True)

file = "HVC_test.fits"
hdul = fits.open(file)
hdr = hdul[0].header
wcs = WCS(hdr)
data = hdul[0].data
data = np.nan_to_num(data)
print("data.shape =", data.shape)

delta_v = abs(hdr['CDELT3']) / 1000
print(delta_v)

cube = sc.read(hdul)
cube = cube.with_spectral_unit(u.km / u.s)

filtered_data = sigma_clip(data, sigma=3, maxiters=10, masked=True)
mask = filtered_data.mask
index = np.transpose(np.nonzero(mask)).astype(int)

db = DBSCAN(eps=np.sqrt(3), min_samples=18, n_jobs=-1).fit(index)
labels = db.labels_
unique_labels = set(labels)
n_clusters = len(unique_labels) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)

# use numpy array to calculate moment 0

def moment_0_np(data, index, labels, n_clusters):
    moment_0_cube = np.empty(0)
    for i in trange(n_clusters):
        vyx = index[labels == i]  # the vyx coord of every point in cluster_i
        bool_array = np.zeros(data.shape, dtype=np.bool)
        bool_array[vyx[:,0], vyx[:,1], vyx[:,2]] = True  # set True for every point in cluster_i
        moment_0_coo = sp.coo_array(np.nansum(bool_array * data * delta_v, axis=0))
    moment_0_cube = np.hstack((moment_0_cube, moment_0_coo))
    return moment_0_cube

moment_0_cube_np = moment_0_np(data, index, labels, n_clusters)
print(moment_0_cube_np[0])

# use spectral cube to calculate moment 0

def moment_0_sc(data, index, labels, n_clusters):
    moment_0_cube = np.empty(0)
    for i in trange(n_clusters):
        vyx = index[labels == i]  # the vyx coord of every point in cluster_i
        bool_array = np.zeros(data.shape, dtype=np.bool)
        bool_array[vyx[:,0], vyx[:,1], vyx[:,2]] = True  # set True for every point in cluster_i
        bool_cube = sc(bool_array * data, wcs=wcs).with_spectral_unit(u.km / u.s)
        moment_0_coo = sp.coo_array(bool_cube.moment(order=0))
    moment_0_cube = np.hstack((moment_0_cube, moment_0_coo))
    return moment_0_cube

moment_0_cube_sc = moment_0_sc(data, index, labels, n_clusters)
print(moment_0_cube_sc[0])

print(moment_0_cube_np[0] - moment_0_cube_sc[0])

As @keflavich said, when working with 32-bit floats, the numerical precision will be limited to ~1e-8.

The straightforward aspect is that the first computation using `delta_v = abs(hdr['CDELT3']) / 1000` results in an array of 32-bit floats (`COOrdinate sparse array of dtype 'float32'`), while using `delta_v = (abs(hdr['CDELT3']) * u.m / u.s).to(u.km / u.s).value` results in an array of 64-bit floats (`COOrdinate sparse array of dtype 'float64'`).  For an accurate/consistent calculation, you simply need to make sure that your float array is 64 bits before doing any summing.  One way could be to convert the original data array to avoid any misunderstanding:
```
data = data.astype(np.float64)
```

The surprising aspect is _why_ these two expressions for `delta_v` lead to different behavior, and it's a "problem" with NumPy.  `delta_v` is a 64-bit float in both cases, but in the first case it is native Python `float` and in the second case it is a NumPy `float64`.  The problem then is triggered by the `data * delta_v` product later, where data is an array of `np.float32`

* a `np.float32` times a Python `float` stays a `np.float32`
* a `np.float32` times a Python `np.float64` becomes a `np.float64`

In other words, the first expression would behave how you want if you simply cast `delta_v` to be a NumPy 64-bit float rather than a Python float:
```
delta_v = np.float64(abs(hdr['CDELT3']) / 1000)

from astropy.wcs import WCS
from spectral_cube import SpectralCube as sc
import astropy.units as u

np.seterr(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore")

file = "HVC_test.fits"

delta_v = abs(hdr['CDELT3']) / 1000

labels = db.labels_
unique_labels = set(labels)
n_clusters = len(unique_labels) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)

# use numpy array to calculate moment 0

def moment_0_np(data, index, labels, n_clusters):
    moment_0_cube = np.empty(0)
    for i in trange(n_clusters):
        vyx = index[labels == i]  # the vyx coord of every point in cluster_i
        bool_array = np.zeros(data.shape, dtype=np.bool)
        bool_array[vyx[:,0], vyx[:,1], vyx[:,2]] = True  # set True for every point in cluster_i
        moment_0_coo = sp.coo_array(np.nansum(bool_array * data * delta_v, axis=0))
    moment_0_cube = np.hstack((moment_0_cube, moment_0_coo))
    return moment_0_cube

moment_0_cube_np = moment_0_np(data, index, labels, n_clusters)
print(moment_0_cube_np[0])

# use spectral cube to calculate moment 0

def moment_0_sc(data, index, labels, n_clusters):
    moment_0_cube = np.empty(0)
    for i in trange(n_clusters):
        vyx = index[labels == i]  # the vyx coord of every point in cluster_i
        bool_array = np.zeros(data.shape, dtype=np.bool)
        bool_array[vyx[:,0], vyx[:,1], vyx[:,2]] = True  # set True for every point in cluster_i
        bool_cube = sc(bool_array * data, wcs=wcs).with_spectral_unit(u.km / u.s)
        moment_0_coo = sp.coo_array(bool_cube.moment(order=0))
    moment_0_cube = np.hstack((moment_0_cube, moment_0_coo))
    return moment_0_cube

moment_0_cube_sc = moment_0_sc(data, index, labels, n_clusters)
print(moment_0_cube_sc[0])

print(moment_0_cube_np[0] - moment_0_cube_sc[0])

import numpy as np

from tqdm import trange
from astropy.wcs import WCS
from spectral_cube import SpectralCube as sc
import astropy.units as u

np.seterr(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore")
np.set_printoptions(precision=12, suppress=True)

file = "HVC_test.fits"

hdr = hdul[0].header
wcs = WCS(hdr)
data = hdul[0].data
data = np.nan_to_num(data)
print("data.shape =", data.shape)

delta_v = abs(hdr['CDELT3']) / 1000
print(delta_v)

cube = sc.read(hdul)
cube = cube.with_spectral_unit(u.km / u.s)

filtered_data = sigma_clip(data, sigma=3, maxiters=10, masked=True)

labels = db.labels_
unique_labels = set(labels)
n_clusters = len(unique_labels) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)

# use numpy array to calculate moment 0

def moment_0_np(data, index, labels, n_clusters):
    moment_0_cube = np.empty(0)
    for i in trange(n_clusters):
        vyx = index[labels == i]  # the vyx coord of every point in cluster_i
        bool_array = np.zeros(data.shape, dtype=np.bool)
        bool_array[vyx[:,0], vyx[:,1], vyx[:,2]] = True  # set True for every point in cluster_i
        moment_0_coo = sp.coo_array(np.nansum(bool_array * data * delta_v, axis=0))
    moment_0_cube = np.hstack((moment_0_cube, moment_0_coo))
    return moment_0_cube

moment_0_cube_np = moment_0_np(data, index, labels, n_clusters)
print(moment_0_cube_np[0])

# use spectral cube to calculate moment 0

def moment_0_sc(data, index, labels, n_clusters):
    moment_0_cube = np.empty(0)
    for i in trange(n_clusters):
        vyx = index[labels == i]  # the vyx coord of every point in cluster_i
        bool_array = np.zeros(data.shape, dtype=np.bool)
        bool_array[vyx[:,0], vyx[:,1], vyx[:,2]] = True  # set True for every point in cluster_i
        bool_cube = sc(bool_array * data, wcs=wcs).with_spectral_unit(u.km / u.s)
        moment_0_coo = sp.coo_array(bool_cube.moment(order=0))
    moment_0_cube = np.hstack((moment_0_cube, moment_0_coo))
    return moment_0_cube

moment_0_cube_sc = moment_0_sc(data, index, labels, n_clusters)
print(moment_0_cube_sc[0])

print(moment_0_cube_np[0] - moment_0_cube_sc[0])

+import warnings
+from typing import NamedTuple
+
+import numpy as np
+
+import astropy
+import astropy.units as u
+from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord
+
+from sunpy.sun.models import differential_rotation
+from sunpy.util.exceptions import SunpyUserWarning
+
+from sunkit_image.coalignment.decorators import REGISTERED_METHODS
+
+__all__ = ["AffineParams"]
+
+
+class AffineParams(NamedTuple):
+    """
+    A 2-element tuple containing scale values defining the image scaling along
+    the x and y axes.
+    """
+    scale: tuple[float, float]
+    """
+    A 2x2 matrix defining the rotation transformation of the image.
+    """
+    rotation_matrix: tuple[tuple[float, float], tuple[float, float]]
+    """
+    A 2-element tuple stores the translation of the image along the x and y
+    axes.
+    """
+    translation: tuple[float, float]
+
+
+def _update_fits_wcs_metadata(reference_map, target_map, affine_params):
+    """
+    Update the metadata of a sunpy.map.Map` based on affine transformation
+    parameters.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    reference_map : `sunpy.map.Map`
+        The reference map object to which the target map is to be coaligned.
+    target_map : `sunpy.map.Map`
+        The original map object whose metadata is to be updated.
+    affine_params : `NamedTuple`
+        A `NamedTuple` containing the affine transformation parameters.
+        If you want to use a custom object, it must have attributes for "translation" (dx, dy), "scale", and "rotation_matrix".
+
+    Returns
+    -------
+    `sunpy.map.Map`
+        A new sunpy map object with updated metadata reflecting the affine transformation.
+    """
+    # Updating the PC_ij matrix
+    new_pc_matrix = target_map.rotation_matrix @ affine_params.rotation_matrix
+    # Calculate the new reference pixel.
+    old_reference_pixel = np.asarray([target_map.reference_pixel.x.value, target_map.reference_pixel.y.value])
+    new_reference_pixel = affine_params.scale * affine_params.rotation_matrix @ old_reference_pixel + affine_params.translation
+    reference_coord = reference_map.wcs.pixel_to_world(new_reference_pixel[0],new_reference_pixel[1])
+    Txshift = reference_coord.Tx - target_map.reference_coordinate.Tx
+    Tyshift = reference_coord.Ty - target_map.reference_coordinate.Ty
+
+    # Create a new map with the updated metadata
+    fixed_map = target_map.shift_reference_coord(Txshift, Tyshift)
+    fixed_map.meta["PC1_1"] = new_pc_matrix[0, 0]
+    fixed_map.meta["PC1_2"] = new_pc_matrix[0, 1]
+    fixed_map.meta["PC2_1"] = new_pc_matrix[1, 0]
+    fixed_map.meta["PC2_2"] = new_pc_matrix[1, 1]
+    fixed_map.meta['cdelt1'] = (target_map.scale[0] / affine_params.scale[0]).value
+    fixed_map.meta['cdelt2'] = (target_map.scale[1] / affine_params.scale[1]).value
+    return fixed_map
+
+
+def _warn_user_of_separation(reference_map, target_map):
+    """
+    Issues a warning if the separation between the ``reference_map`` and
+    ``target_map`` is large.
+
+    Parameters
+    ----------
+    reference_map : `sunpy.map.Map`
+        The reference map to which the target map is to be coaligned.
+    target_map : `sunpy.map.Map`
+        The target map to be coaligned to the reference map.
+    """
+    # Maximum angular separation allowed between the reference and target maps
+    tolerable_angular_separation = 1*u.deg
+    ref_coord = SkyCoord(reference_map.observer_coordinate)
+    target_coord = SkyCoord(target_map.observer_coordinate)
+    if astropy.__version__ >= "6.1.0":
+        angular_separation = ref_coord.separation(target_coord, origin_mismatch="ignore")
+    else:
+        angular_separation = ref_coord.separation(target_coord)
+    if angular_separation > tolerable_angular_separation:
+        warnings.warn(
+            "The angular separation between the reference and target maps is large. "
+            "This could cause errors when calculating shift between two "
+            "images. Please make sure the maps are close in space.",
+            SunpyUserWarning,
+            stacklevel=3,
+        )
+    # Calculate time difference and convert to separation angle
+    ref_time = reference_map.date
+    target_time = target_map.date
+    time_diff = abs(ref_time - target_time)

+    if time_separation_angle > tolerable_angular_separation:
+        warnings.warn(
+            "The time difference between the reference and target maps in time is large. "
+            "This could cause errors when calculating shift between two "
+            "images. Please make sure the maps are close in time.",
+            SunpyUserWarning,
+            stacklevel=3,
+        )

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import astropy.units as u
from astropy.wcs import WCS

wcs = WCS({
    'ctype1': 'RA---CAR',
    'ctype2': 'DEC--CAR',
    'crval1': 0,
    'crval2': 0,
    'cdelt1': -1,
    'cdelt2': 1,
    'crpix1': 1,
    'crpix2': 1,
})

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection=wcs)

ax.coords[0].set_ticks(spacing=0.25*u.hourangle)
ax.coords[0].set_ticklabel(rotation=90, pad=25)
ax.coords[0].set_ticklabel_position('bt')

ax.coords[1].set_ticks(spacing=0.25*u.deg)
ax.coords[1].set_ticklabel_position('lr')

ax.set_xlim(-30, 30)
ax.set_ylim(-2, 2)
ax.set_aspect(15)
ax.grid()

plt.show()
```
![download (14)](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/673d6f7a-b13b-486d-8ed9-02a1f4abac1a)

Be aware that currently the tick labels are simplified by essentially traversing the outer frame in a loop: bottom-left corner to bottom-right corner to top-right corner to top-left corner to bottom-left corner.  That means tick labels on opposite sides of the plot are simplified differently.  One could change the (default) traversal strategy so that at least the sides match.

A step further could be to change the (default) traversal direction to match the direction of increasing tick values.  That would prevent some of the oddities seen above, at least for positive tick values.  However, negative tick values make that more challenging, so one might want to split the traversal so that the simplification can go in the direction of increasing tick absolute values.

Even then, I don't know how to best simplify across zero. The automatic simplification of WCSAxes tick labels – typically removes repeated whole degrees or hour angles – can result in confusing tick labels.  Consider for example this plot directly from the current docs:

![ticks_labels_grid-10](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3727f010-c1d5-43cf-b143-34f7d6d79234)

This PR provides the user a way to turn off the simplification by specifying `simplify=False` to `set_ticklabel()` (at the expense of longer tick labels):

![ticks_labels_grid-11](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b490205a-c46b-4a2c-96fd-6d8241dc7453)

The docstring for `CoordinateHelper.set_major_formatter()` claims that the method can accept a matplotlib `Formatter` instance, but that input type simply raises a `NotImplementedError`, and has done so for the past 11 years.  How to implement support for a matplotlib `Formatter` instance is non-obvious, so it makes sense that this aspirational claim has never been made real.  This PR fixes the docstring, but retains the aspiration as a TODO comment for some enterprising developer in the future.

I don't know whether a changelog entry is even warranted here.

Motivated by [this discussion thread](https://community.openastronomy.org/t/add-sign-for-positive-values-in-declination/1105), this PR adds the ability to specify that WCSAxes tick labels always include the sign (namely for positive values).  This behavior is enabled by prefixing the format string provided to `set_major_formatter()` with a `+` character.

Example:
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy.wcs import WCS

wcs = WCS({
    'CTYPE1': 'RA---CAR',
    'CTYPE2': 'DEC--CAR',
    'CRPIX1': 1,
    'CRPIX2': 1,
    'CDELT1': 1,
    'CDELT2': 1,
    'CRVAL1': 0,
    'CRVAL2': 0,
})

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection=wcs)
ax.coords[0].set_major_formatter('+hh')
ax.coords[1].set_major_formatter('+dd')
ax.set_xlim(-151, 149)
ax.set_ylim(-11, 9)
ax.set_title("Always have sign on tick labels")
plt.show()
```

Motivated by [this discussion thread](https://community.openastronomy.org/t/add-sign-for-positive-values-in-declination/1105), this PR adds the ability to specify that WCSAxes tick labels always include the sign (namely for positive values).  This behavior is enabled by prefixing the format string provided to `set_major_formatter()` with a `+` character.

Example:
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy.wcs import WCS

wcs = WCS({
    'CTYPE1': 'RA---CAR',
    'CTYPE2': 'DEC--CAR',
    'CRPIX1': 1,
    'CRPIX2': 1,
    'CDELT1': 1,
    'CDELT2': 1,
    'CRVAL1': 0,
    'CRVAL2': 0,
})

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection=wcs)
ax.coords[0].set_major_formatter('+hh')
ax.coords[1].set_major_formatter('+dd')
ax.set_xlim(-151, 149)
ax.set_ylim(-11, 9)
ax.set_title("Always have sign on tick labels")
plt.show()
```

Motivated by [this discussion thread](https://community.openastronomy.org/t/add-sign-for-positive-values-in-declination/1105), this PR adds the ability to specify that WCSAxes tick labels always include the sign (namely for positive values).  This behavior is enabled by prefixing the format string provided to `set_major_formatter()` with a `+` character.

Example:
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy.wcs import WCS

wcs = WCS({
    'CTYPE1': 'RA---CAR',
    'CTYPE2': 'DEC--CAR',
    'CRPIX1': 1,
    'CRPIX2': 1,
    'CDELT1': 1,
    'CDELT2': 1,
    'CRVAL1': 0,
    'CRVAL2': 0,
})

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection=wcs)
ax.coords[0].set_major_formatter('+hh')
ax.coords[1].set_major_formatter('+dd')
ax.set_xlim(-151, 149)
ax.set_ylim(-11, 9)
ax.set_title("Always have sign on tick labels")
plt.show()
```

Motivated by [this discussion thread](https://community.openastronomy.org/t/add-sign-for-positive-values-in-declination/1105), this PR adds the ability to specify that WCSAxes tick labels always include the sign (namely for positive values).  This behavior is enabled by prefixing the format string provided to `set_major_formatter()` with a `+` character.

Example:
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from astropy.wcs import WCS

wcs = WCS({
    'CTYPE1': 'RA---CAR',
    'CTYPE2': 'DEC--CAR',
    'CRPIX1': 1,
    'CRPIX2': 1,
    'CDELT1': 1,
    'CDELT2': 1,
    'CRVAL1': 0,
    'CRVAL2': 0,
})

fig = plt.figure()
ax = fig.add_subplot(projection=wcs)
ax.coords[0].set_major_formatter('+hh')
ax.coords[1].set_major_formatter('+dd')
ax.set_xlim(-151, 149)
ax.set_ylim(-11, 9)
ax.set_title("Always have sign on tick labels")
plt.show()
```

(See #1736 for a past attempt.)  The tricky aspect is negotiating between the natural component of impact angle, which is 0 degrees at disk center, and the FITS-WCS component of declination, which is –90 degrees at disk center.  The PR adds:

Describe the bug

Not sure if this is an astropy or sunpy bug (or user error).

If I make a plot with `WCSAxes` and do a coordinate overlay of helioprojective coordinates, it looks like the helioprojective grid is in degrees, but it's marked as arcseconds.

I'm not sure how to make a WCS with a builtin frame and get the helioprojective origin to be the same, so here's an example with a custom frame that's just helioprojective, but rotated. (I encountered this when using my own custom frame that transforms to helioprojective).
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/a5dd2820-4c82-4933-bd30-0f851564293a)

Note that the custom frame ticks are every five degrees, and the helioprojective overlay ticks have the same spacing, but they're labeled as every 5 arcsec. (And since the custom frame is just rotated helioproejctive coords, the two frames' degrees should be the same size on the plot.)

Swapping which frame is the overlay gives a plot that looks right:
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/543b9005-bc31-451f-8833-106906bcaf25)

I wonder if this has to do with helioprojective using arcsec as its default unit.

### To Reproduce

```python
import astropy.coordinates
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.wcs import WCS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import sunpy.coordinates

#
# Create a frame that transforms to helioprojective
#

class TiltedFrame(astropy.coordinates.BaseCoordinateFrame):
    """
    This is a Helioprojective frame, but rotated 20 degrees around the Sun--observer axis
    """

Describe the bug

Not sure if this is an astropy or sunpy bug (or user error).

If I make a plot with `WCSAxes` and do a coordinate overlay of helioprojective coordinates, it looks like the helioprojective grid is in degrees, but it's marked as arcseconds.

I'm not sure how to make a WCS with a builtin frame and get the helioprojective origin to be the same, so here's an example with a custom frame that's just helioprojective, but rotated. (I encountered this when using my own custom frame that transforms to helioprojective).
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/a5dd2820-4c82-4933-bd30-0f851564293a)

Note that the custom frame ticks are every five degrees, and the helioprojective overlay ticks have the same spacing, but they're labeled as every 5 arcsec. (And since the custom frame is just rotated helioproejctive coords, the two frames' degrees should be the same size on the plot.)

Swapping which frame is the overlay gives a plot that looks right:
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/543b9005-bc31-451f-8833-106906bcaf25)

I wonder if this has to do with helioprojective using arcsec as its default unit.

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

The reason that #7758 breaks differential_rotate() is because it chooses to return the output map as the same subclass as input map, but it of course has no idea how to correctly modify the metadata so that the source subclass understands the new reference time. All the function modifies is DATE-OBS. For AIAMap, differential_rotate() would need to modify T_OBS. (Even for subclasses that do not override .reference_date, if the input metadata has DATE-AVG, differential_rotate() would need to modify DATE-AVG.) Thus, the output map has the wrong

Okay, I'm thinking we add ._set_date() and ._set_reference_date() methods to GenericMap, and any subclass that overrides .date/.reference_date needs to override the corresponding setter as well.reference time, which triggers a transformation of the bounding box that isn't supposed to happen, which triggers the submap warning for off-disk corners.

Fixes https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/issues/7757

+.. _sunpy-how-to-create-custom-coordinate-objects:
+
+**********************************************
+Create Coordinate Objects with Custom Observer
+**********************************************
+
+It is possible to specify an observer other than Earth by providing a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` object representing the observer's location.
+This can be useful when working with data from instruments located at specific points in space, such as spacecraft.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, CartesianRepresentation
+    >>> from sunpy.coordinates import frames
+    >>> import astropy.units as u
+
+Define the observer's position in Heliocentric coordinates
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(-100*u.arcsec, 500*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective)
+    >>> observer_coord= SkyCoord(x=-72241.0*u.km, y=361206.1*u.km, z=589951.4*u.km, frame=frames.Heliocentric)","path":"docs/how_to/create_custom_coords.rst","commit_id":"a72db4b88e84d7e3a099dad54273cfc855e215d2","original_commit_id":"a72db4b88e84d7e3a099dad54273cfc855e215d2","user":{"login":"ayshih","id":991759,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjk5MTc1OQ==","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/991759?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih","html_url":"https://github.com/ayshih","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"body":"```suggestion

+.. _sunpy-how-to-create-custom-coordinate-objects:
+
+**********************************************
+Create Coordinate Objects with Custom Observer
+**********************************************
+
+It is possible to specify an observer other than Earth by providing a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` object representing the observer's location.
+This can be useful when working with data from instruments located at specific points in space, such as spacecraft.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, CartesianRepresentation
+    >>> from sunpy.coordinates import frames
+    >>> import astropy.units as u
+
+Define the observer's position in Heliocentric coordinates
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(-100*u.arcsec, 500*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective)
+    >>> observer_coord= SkyCoord(x=-72241.0*u.km, y=361206.1*u.km, z=589951.4*u.km, frame=frames.Heliocentric)
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(70*u.deg, -30*u.deg, frame=frames.HeliographicStonyhurst)
+    >>> observer_coord
+    <SkyCoord (HeliographicStonyhurst: obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km): (lon, lat) in deg
+        (70., -30.)>","path":"docs/how_to/create_custom_coords.rst","commit_id":"a72db4b88e84d7e3a099dad54273cfc855e215d2","original_commit_id":"a72db4b88e84d7e3a099dad54273cfc855e215d2","user":{"login":"ayshih","id":991759,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjk5MTc1OQ==","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/991759?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih","html_url":"https://github.com/ayshih","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/ayshih/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"body":"```suggestion

+.. _sunpy-how-to-create-custom-coordinate-objects:
+
+**********************************************
+Create Coordinate Objects with Custom Observer
+**********************************************
+
+It is possible to specify an observer other than Earth by providing a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` object representing the observer's location.
+This can be useful when working with data from instruments located at specific points in space, such as spacecraft.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, CartesianRepresentation
+    >>> from sunpy.coordinates import frames
+    >>> import astropy.units as u
+
+Define the observer's position in Heliocentric coordinates
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(-100*u.arcsec, 500*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective)
+    >>> observer_coord= SkyCoord(x=-72241.0*u.km, y=361206.1*u.km, z=589951.4*u.km, frame=frames.Heliocentric)
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(70*u.deg, -30*u.deg, frame=frames.HeliographicStonyhurst)
+    >>> observer_coord
+    <SkyCoord (HeliographicStonyhurst: obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km): (lon, lat) in deg
+        (70., -30.)>
+

+.. _sunpy-how-to-create-custom-coordinate-objects:
+
+**********************************************
+Create Coordinate Objects with Custom Observer
+**********************************************
+
+It is possible to specify an observer other than Earth by providing a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` object representing the observer's location.
+This can be useful when working with data from instruments located at specific points in space, such as spacecraft.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, CartesianRepresentation
+    >>> from sunpy.coordinates import frames
+    >>> import astropy.units as u
+
+Define the observer's position in Heliocentric coordinates
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(-100*u.arcsec, 500*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective)
+    >>> observer_coord= SkyCoord(x=-72241.0*u.km, y=361206.1*u.km, z=589951.4*u.km, frame=frames.Heliocentric)
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(70*u.deg, -30*u.deg, frame=frames.HeliographicStonyhurst)
+    >>> observer_coord
+    <SkyCoord (HeliographicStonyhurst: obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km): (lon, lat) in deg
+        (70., -30.)>
+
+Create a coordinate in Helioprojective with the custom observer
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> coord = SkyCoord(100*u.arcsec, 200*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective, observer=observer_coord)
+    >>> coord
+    <SkyCoord (Helioprojective: obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km, observer=<HeliographicStonyhurst Coordinate (obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km): (lon, lat, radius) in (deg, deg, km)
+        (70., -30., 695700.)>): (Tx, Ty) in arcsec
+        (100., 200.)>
+
+In this example, we define the observer's position at ``-100*u.arcsec`` along the x-axis and ``500*u.arcsec`` along y-axis in Heliocentric coordinates.

+.. _sunpy-how-to-create-custom-coordinate-objects:
+
+**********************************************
+Create Coordinate Objects with Custom Observer
+**********************************************
+
+It is possible to specify an observer other than Earth by providing a `~astropy.coordinates.SkyCoord` object representing the observer's location.
+This can be useful when working with data from instruments located at specific points in space, such as spacecraft.
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, CartesianRepresentation
+    >>> from sunpy.coordinates import frames
+    >>> import astropy.units as u
+
+Define the observer's position in Heliocentric coordinates
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(-100*u.arcsec, 500*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective)
+    >>> observer_coord= SkyCoord(x=-72241.0*u.km, y=361206.1*u.km, z=589951.4*u.km, frame=frames.Heliocentric)
+    >>> observer_coord = SkyCoord(70*u.deg, -30*u.deg, frame=frames.HeliographicStonyhurst)
+    >>> observer_coord
+    <SkyCoord (HeliographicStonyhurst: obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km): (lon, lat) in deg
+        (70., -30.)>
+
+Create a coordinate in Helioprojective with the custom observer
+
+.. code-block:: python
+
+    >>> coord = SkyCoord(100*u.arcsec, 200*u.arcsec, frame=frames.Helioprojective, observer=observer_coord)
+    >>> coord
+    <SkyCoord (Helioprojective: obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km, observer=<HeliographicStonyhurst Coordinate (obstime=None, rsun=695700.0 km): (lon, lat, radius) in (deg, deg, km)

pull request is to address the fact that coordinate frames cannot be written to tables (with or without data). It does this in two commits:
1. Let BaseCoordinateFrame have an `.info` attribute. Here, since the code is almost the same as that for SkyCoord, I base `SkyCoordInfo` on the new `CoordinateFrameInfo`.  Also, to avoid duplication of `.insert` methods, I define an `_insert` method on the info class, which can be used for both `BaseCoordinateFrame` and `SkyCoord`.
2. Allow the use of `BaseCoordinateFrame` in tables, including tests for `SkyOffsetFrame` with and without associated data. 

To get this to work, `Table` can no longer rely on the input having a `len` - since data-less coordinate frames raise on that. So, instead it prefers `col.shape[0]` if that is available. Obviously, instead one could give data-less frames a `len`, but that seemed a rather big API change (even though it is perhaps reasonable). Furthermore, since `SkyOffsetFrame` classes are defined on the fly, I treat these as special cases in the white list of allowed classes for serialization.

The WCS of the file @keflavich shared has:
```
WCS Keywords

Number of WCS axes: 2
CTYPE : 'GLON-CAR' 'GLAT-CAR'
CRVAL : 180.0 0.0
CRPIX : 1.0 241.0
PC1_1 PC1_2  : 1.0 0.0
PC2_1 PC2_2  : 0.0 1.0
CDELT : -0.125 0.125
NAXIS : 2881  481
```
The "problem" is that the reference pixel in the longitude direction (CRPIX1) is not in the center of the data array (here, 1 instead of 1441) and `wcslib` for cylindrical projections (currently) always centers the 360 degrees of longitude on the reference pixel (i.e., 180 degrees on either side of CRVAL1).  Thus, when the WCS has CRPIX1 all the way to one side, half of the longitudes fall off of the data array (which is why `wcs_world2pix()` returns a negative pixel index) and half of the data array is "missing" longitudes (which is why `wcs_pix2world()` returns NaNs).

Barring changes to `wcslib` to make it more smart, the workaround is to redefine CRPIX1 so that it is in the center of the data array (here, 1441 instead of 1) and update CRVAL1 accordingly (here, 0.0 instead of 180.0).  For a CAR projection, there should be no difference in the world<->pixel mapping, but now the WCS handles longitudes as desired:
![Figure_2](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/3f16af70-205b-4206-b53e-d1d2415b2bd0)

Describe the bug

sunpy.coordinatess.sun.orientation calculates (according to its doc-string) "the orientation angle for the Sun from a specified Earth location and time. The orientation angle is the angle between local zenith and solar north, measured eastward from local zenith."  

Currently, the calculation applies only to a targeted coordinated centered on solar disk center; although this angle does change as a function of targeted locations away from disk center.   Therefore, an associated feature request would be to extend this calculation to non-disk-center targets. 

That said, there is likely an error in the currently implementation (even when limited to disk center).  The code calls the _sun_north_angle_to_z function that projects a few vectors into the sky and measures the angles between them.  However, the vector used for the zenith direction is always one directed from the <cartesian representation of the disk center sky coordinates> to the <zenith cartesian representation coordinates at (0,0,1)>.  Because the zenith is always defined as (0,0,1),  there is an issue when projecting this vector onto the spherical projection of the sky local to the target instead.   An improved approach would be to define a vector to the zenith direction based on a small angle difference from the target coordinates in the +Altitude direction of an AltAz frame.  The differences between these calculations can be as large as a few degrees.  

So, this ticket requests first an improved algorithm be considered for the calculation of this angle, and perhaps then an extension to non-disk center pointing.  

Note also that the docstring could be more specific in the definition of this angle and its reference direction.

### To Reproduce

## HERE IS A CODE SNIPPET TO SHOW THE ERROR AND A CANDIDATE IMPLEMENTATION OF A SOLUTION 
```

import os
import glob
import numpy as np

import matplotlib.dates as mdates
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.io import fits 
from astropy.time import Time
from astropy.wcs import WCS
from astropy.coordinates import SkyCoord, EarthLocation, AltAz,CartesianRepresentation
from sunpy.coordinates import sun, HeliocentricInertial, Helioprojective,GeocentricEarthEquatorial
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
%matplotlib inline
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm
plt.rcParams.update({'figure.max_open_warning': 0})
plt.rcParams["image.origin"] = 'lower'
plt.rcParams["image.cmap"] = 'gray'
plt.rcParams["image.interpolation"] = 'nearest'

dkist = EarthLocation(lat=20.7067*u.deg, lon=203.7436*u.deg, height=3067*u.m)
obstimes = Time('2024-06-27 17:00') + np.arange(0., 12,0.1)*u.hour
sunpy_orientation = sun.orientation(location = dkist,time = obstimes).deg

sunpy_orientation[0]

results = np.zeros(len(obstimes))
for nn,t0 in enumerate(obstimes):
    frame_altaz = AltAz(obstime=t0, location=dkist)
    x,y = 0,0
    target_coords = SkyCoord(x*u.arcsec,y*u.arcsec,obstime = t0,observer = 'earth',frame = "helioprojective").transform_to(frame_altaz)
    ## coordinates of a point 1 arcsec to the solar north or boresight used to calculate the solar 
    ## orientation angle at this alt az value (note this is not the same as at disk center) 
    ptCoord = SkyCoord(x*u.arcsec,(y+1)*u.arcsec,obstime=t0, observer='earth', frame="helioprojective")
    
    ## transform to altaz frame (handling case if the point is offlimb)
    with Helioprojective.assume_spherical_screen(target_coords.observer):
        target_altaz = target_coords.transform_to(frame_altaz) 
        ptCoord_altaz = ptCoord.transform_to(frame_altaz) 
        toZenith_altaz = SkyCoord(target_altaz.az,target_altaz.alt + 1*u.arcsec,target_altaz.distance,frame = frame_altaz)
    
    # Use cross products to obtain the sky projections of the two vectors (rotated by 90 deg)
    sky_normal = target_altaz.data.to_cartesian()
    pt_normal  = ptCoord_altaz.data.to_cartesian()
    zen_normal = toZenith_altaz.data.to_cartesian()
    
    ## project zenith direction and direction to observed point into sky
    z_in_sky = zen_normal.cross(sky_normal)
    pt_in_sky = pt_normal.cross(sky_normal)
    
    # Normalize directional vectors
    sky_normal /= sky_normal.norm()
    pt_normal  /= pt_normal.norm()
    pt_in_sky  /= pt_in_sky.norm()
    z_in_sky   /= z_in_sky.norm()
    
    # Calculate the signed angle between the two projected vectors
    ## angle between to zenith and to point from center 
    cos_theta = pt_in_sky.dot(z_in_sky)
    sin_theta = pt_in_sky.cross(z_in_sky).dot(sky_normal)
    solar_orientation = np.arctan2(sin_theta, cos_theta)
    results[nn] = solar_orientation.to(u.deg).value

from mpl_toolkits.axes_grid1.inset_locator import zoomed_inset_axes,mark_inset

import pytz
HST = pytz.timezone('US/Hawaii')
plt.rcParams["timezone"] = pytz.timezone('US/Hawaii').zone

fig,ax = plt.subplots(2,1,figsize = (5,5),sharex=True)
ax[0].plot(obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST),sunpy_orientation,lw = 0.4,label = 'Sunpy Orientation Angle')
ax[0].plot(obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST),results,'k',lw = 0.4,label = 'Proposed Improvement')
myFmt = mdates.DateFormatter('%H:%M')
ax[0].xaxis.set_major_formatter(myFmt)
ax[0].set_ylim(-180,180)

ax[1].plot(obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST),sunpy_orientation- results,'k',label = '(Sunpy - Improved)')
ax[1].set_xlabel("Time [HST] (2024-06-27)")
ax[0].set_ylabel("Degrees")
ax[1].set_ylabel("Degrees")

axins = zoomed_inset_axes(ax[0],3.5,loc='lower right')
axins.plot(obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST),sunpy_orientation,lw = 0.4,label = 'Sunpy Orientation Angle')
axins.plot(obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST),results,'k',lw = 0.4,label = 'Proposed Improvement')
axins.set_xlim(obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST)[110],obstimes.to_datetime(timezone=HST)[119])
axins.set_ylim(60,85)
axins.xaxis.set_visible(False)
mark_inset(ax[0],axins,loc1=1,loc2=2)

ax[0].legend(loc = 'upper left')
ax[1].legend(loc = 'upper left')
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig('sunpy_orient_vs_newCalc.png',dpi = 300)

+New `~sunpy.coordinates.PlanarScreen` context manager
+=====================================================
+
+`~sunpy.coordinates.PlanarScreen` provides a context manager for interpreting 2D coordinates as being on the inside of a planar screen.
+The plane goes through Sun center (or some specified distance from Sun center) and is perpendicular to the vector between the specified vantage point and Sun center.
+This replaces the default assumption where 2D coordinates are mapped onto the surface of the Sun and is an alternative to `~sunpy.coordinates.SphericalScreen`.
+
+Deprecate `~sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective.assume_spherical_screen`
+======================================================================
+

Description

I am not sure whether this is a bug in Astropy or in [APLPy](https://github.com/aplpy/aplpy): with Astropy 6.1.1, I get [test failures](https://ci.debian.net/packages/a/aplpy/testing/amd64/48397735/) of APLPy 2.1.0, for example:
```
 _____________________________ test_beam_add_remove _____________________________
    def test_beam_add_remove():
>       f = FITSFigure(HDU)
[…]
>           equinox = "{:g}".format(FK5.equinox.jyear)
E           AttributeError: 'TimeAttribute' object has no attribute 'jyear'
 
/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages/aplpy/axis_labels.py:47: AttributeError
```
This is a regression; the same tests work well with Astropy 6.0.0.

As **FK5** is a class (which I'd expect to have constant attributes), and I didn't find anything about **jyear** or **TimeAttribute** in the Changelog, and also not in a (very quick) review of the changes, I could imagine that is "somehow" a bug in Astropy. FK5 is directly imported on top of [`axis_labels.py`](https://github.com/aplpy/aplpy/blob/00bbe28bea179b120e39818a9f171159b51333e4/aplpy/axis_labels.py).

What makes it more confusing is that one finds a [few tests](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/blob/13d314c53a28759983b40c91e31bf08dbfe378f2/astropy/coordinates/tests/test_arrays.py#L191) that use **fk5.equinox.jyear** (accessed from an **FK5** object, however; not from the **FK5** class), so I am not sure whether this is a bug in Astropy or APLPy wrongly used the class before and this is now uncovered. Please transform the issue to APLPy if this is an issue there.

Cc @astrofrog as APLPy maintainer

### Expected behavior

I'd guess the test  should succeed.

### How to Reproduce

Run the pytest of APLPy

### Versions

* Debian testing
* APLPy 2.1.0
* Astropy 6.1.1
* numpy 1.26.4
* matplotlib 3.6.3

Depending on your perspective, a clearer workaround might be `FK5.equinox.default.jyear`.  That is, instead of instantiating the class, you just need to explicitly retrieve the default value for the frame attribute when accessed on the frame class.

> let me ping @ayshih to see if he has a suggestion on how we can fix this regression while not losing the benefit of having a sensible docstring

I don't have any bright ideas.  The tricky aspect is that there are two types of frame-attribute defaults.  The default J2000.0 for the `equinox` frame attribute on `FK5` is correct in all but the most unusual circumstances, so it would be nice to spit that out readily. Describe the bug

Not sure if this is an astropy or sunpy bug (or user error).

If I make a plot with `WCSAxes` and do a coordinate overlay of helioprojective coordinates, it looks like the helioprojective grid is in degrees, but it's marked as arcseconds.

I'm not sure how to make a WCS with a builtin frame and get the helioprojective origin to be the same, so here's an example with a custom frame that's just helioprojective, but rotated. (I encountered this when using my own custom frame that transforms to helioprojective).
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/a5dd2820-4c82-4933-bd30-0f851564293a)

Note that the custom frame ticks are every five degrees, and the helioprojective overlay ticks have the same spacing, but they're labeled as every 5 arcsec. (And since the custom frame is just rotated helioproejctive coords, the two frames' degrees should be the same size on the plot.)

Swapping which frame is the overlay gives a plot that looks right:
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/543b9005-bc31-451f-8833-106906bcaf25)

I wonder if this has to do with helioprojective using arcsec as its default unit.

### To Reproduce

```python
import astropy.coordinates
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.wcs import WCS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import sunpy.coordinates

#
# Create a frame that transforms to helioprojective
#

class TiltedFrame(astropy.coordinates.BaseCoordinateFrame):
    """
    This is a Helioprojective frame, but rotated 20 degrees around the Sun--observer axis
    """
    default_representation = astropy.coordinates.representation.SphericalRepresentation
    obstime = astropy.coordinates.TimeAttribute()
    observer = sunpy.coordinates.frameattributes.ObserverCoordinateAttribute(
        sunpy.coordinates.HeliographicStonyhurst)


@astropy.coordinates.frame_transform_graph.transform(
    astropy.coordinates.DynamicMatrixTransform,
    sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective,
    TiltedFrame)
def hpc_to_tilted(HPcoord, tilted_frame):
    angle = 20*u.deg
    matrix = np.array([[1, 0, 0],
                       [0, np.cos(angle), -np.sin(angle)],
                       [0, np.sin(angle),  np.cos(angle)]])
    return matrix


@astropy.coordinates.frame_transform_graph.transform(
    astropy.coordinates.DynamicMatrixTransform,
    TiltedFrame,
    sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective)
def tilted_to_hpc(tilted_coord, HPframe):
    angle = -20*u.deg
    matrix = np.array([[1, 0, 0],
                       [0, np.cos(angle), -np.sin(angle)],
                       [0, np.sin(angle),  np.cos(angle)]])
    return matrix

#
# Register the frame
#

def tilted_wcs_frame_mapping(wcs):
    ctypes = {c[:4] for c in wcs.wcs.ctype}
    if ({'TLLN', 'TLLT'} <= ctypes):
        dateobs = wcs.wcs.dateavg or wcs.wcs.dateobs or None
        observer = sunpy.coordinates.HeliographicStonyhurst(
            wcs.wcs.aux.hgln_obs * u.deg,
            wcs.wcs.aux.hglt_obs * u.deg,
            wcs.wcs.aux.dsun_obs * u.m)
        return TiltedFrame(observer=observer, obstime=dateobs)
    return None


def tilted_frame_wcs_mapping(frame, projection='TAN'):
    if isinstance(frame, TiltedFrame):
        wcs = astropy.wcs.WCS(naxis=2)
        wcs.wcs.dateobs = frame.obstime.utc.isot
        wcs.wcs.aux.hgln_obs = frame.lon.to_value(u.deg)
        wcs.wcs.aux.hglt_obs = frame.lat.to_value(u.deg)
        wcs.wcs.aux.dsun_obs = frame.radius.to_value(u.m)
        wcs.wcs.ctype = f'TLLN-{projection}', f'TLLT-{projection}'
        wcs.wcs.cunit = ['deg', 'deg']
        return wcs
    return None


astropy.wcs.utils.WCS_FRAME_MAPPINGS.append([tilted_wcs_frame_mapping])
astropy.wcs.utils.FRAME_WCS_MAPPINGS.append([tilted_frame_wcs_mapping])
astropy.wcs.wcsapi.fitswcs.CTYPE_TO_UCD1_CUSTOM.append(
    {
        "TLLN": "custom:pos.tiltedframe.lon",
        "TLLT": "custom:pos.tiltedframe.lat",
    })


#
# Create the "main" WCS for plotting
#

wcs = WCS(naxis=2)
wcs.wcs.ctype = "TLLN-CAR", 'TLLT-CAR'
wcs.wcs.crpix = 100, 100
wcs.wcs.crval = 0, 0
wcs.wcs.cdelt = 0.1, 0.1
wcs.wcs.aux.hgln_obs = 0
wcs.wcs.aux.hglt_obs = 0
wcs.wcs.aux.dsun_obs = u.au.to(u.m)
wcs.wcs.dateobs = "2020-01-01T00:00:00"
wcs.wcs.dateavg = wcs.wcs.dateobs
wcs.fix()


ax = plt.subplot(111, projection=wcs)
plt.imshow(np.zeros((200, 200)))
ax.coords.grid(color='white')
ax.coords[0].set_axislabel("Custom frame X")
ax.coords[1].set_axislabel("Custom frame Y")

overlay = ax.get_coords_overlay('helioprojective')
overlay.grid(color='gold', ls='dotted')
overlay[0].set_axislabel("Helioprojective Tx")
overlay[1].set_axislabel("Helioprojective Ty")
```

Describe the bug

Not sure if this is an astropy or sunpy bug (or user error).

If I make a plot with `WCSAxes` and do a coordinate overlay of helioprojective coordinates, it looks like the helioprojective grid is in degrees, but it's marked as arcseconds.

I'm not sure how to make a WCS with a builtin frame and get the helioprojective origin to be the same, so here's an example with a custom frame that's just helioprojective, but rotated. (I encountered this when using my own custom frame that transforms to helioprojective).
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/a5dd2820-4c82-4933-bd30-0f851564293a)

Note that the custom frame ticks are every five degrees, and the helioprojective overlay ticks have the same spacing, but they're labeled as every 5 arcsec. (And since the custom frame is just rotated helioproejctive coords, the two frames' degrees should be the same size on the plot.)

Swapping which frame is the overlay gives a plot that looks right:
![image](https://github.com/sunpy/sunpy/assets/23462789/543b9005-bc31-451f-8833-106906bcaf25)

I wonder if this has to do with helioprojective using arcsec as its default unit.

### To Reproduce

```python
import astropy.coordinates
import astropy.units as u
from astropy.wcs import WCS
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import sunpy.coordinates

#
# Create a frame that transforms to helioprojective
#

class TiltedFrame(astropy.coordinates.BaseCoordinateFrame):
    """
    This is a Helioprojective frame, but rotated 20 degrees around the Sun--observer axis
    """
    default_representation = astropy.coordinates.representation.SphericalRepresentation
    obstime = astropy.coordinates.TimeAttribute()
    observer = sunpy.coordinates.frameattributes.ObserverCoordinateAttribute(
        sunpy.coordinates.HeliographicStonyhurst)


@astropy.coordinates.frame_transform_graph.transform(
    astropy.coordinates.DynamicMatrixTransform,
    sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective,
    TiltedFrame)
def hpc_to_tilted(HPcoord, tilted_frame):
    angle = 20*u.deg
    matrix = np.array([[1, 0, 0],
                       [0, np.cos(angle), -np.sin(angle)],
                       [0, np.sin(angle),  np.cos(angle)]])
    return matrix


@astropy.coordinates.frame_transform_graph.transform(
    astropy.coordinates.DynamicMatrixTransform,
    TiltedFrame,
    sunpy.coordinates.Helioprojective)
def tilted_to_hpc(tilted_coord, HPframe):
    angle = -20*u.deg
    matrix = np.array([[1, 0, 0],
                       [0, np.cos(angle), -np.sin(angle)],
                       [0, np.sin(angle),  np.cos(angle)]])
    return matrix

#
# Register the frame
#

def tilted_wcs_frame_mapping(wcs):
    ctypes = {c[:4] for c in wcs.wcs.ctype}
    if ({'TLLN', 'TLLT'} <= ctypes):
        dateobs = wcs.wcs.dateavg or wcs.wcs.dateobs or None
        observer = sunpy.coordinates.HeliographicStonyhurst(
            wcs.wcs.aux.hgln_obs * u.deg,
            wcs.wcs.aux.hglt_obs * u.deg,
            wcs.wcs.aux.dsun_obs * u.m)
        return TiltedFrame(observer=observer, obstime=dateobs)
    return None


def tilted_frame_wcs_mapping(frame, projection='TAN'):
    if isinstance(frame, TiltedFrame):
        wcs = astropy.wcs.WCS(naxis=2)
        wcs.wcs.dateobs = frame.obstime.utc.isot
        wcs.wcs.aux.hgln_obs = frame.lon.to_value(u.deg)
        wcs.wcs.aux.hglt_obs = frame.lat.to_value(u.deg)
        wcs.wcs.aux.dsun_obs = frame.radius.to_value(u.m)
        wcs.wcs.ctype = f'TLLN-{projection}', f'TLLT-{projection}'
        wcs.wcs.cunit = ['deg', 'deg']
        return wcs
    return None


astropy.wcs.utils.WCS_FRAME_MAPPINGS.append([tilted_wcs_frame_mapping])
astropy.wcs.utils.FRAME_WCS_MAPPINGS.append([tilted_frame_wcs_mapping])
astropy.wcs.wcsapi.fitswcs.CTYPE_TO_UCD1_CUSTOM.append(
    {
        "TLLN": "custom:pos.tiltedframe.lon",
        "TLLT": "custom:pos.tiltedframe.lat",
    })


#
# Create the "main" WCS for plotting
#

wcs = WCS(naxis=2)
wcs.wcs.ctype = "TLLN-CAR", 'TLLT-CAR'
wcs.wcs.crpix = 100, 100
wcs.wcs.crval = 0, 0
wcs.wcs.cdelt = 0.1, 0.1
wcs.wcs.aux.hgln_obs = 0
wcs.wcs.aux.hglt_obs = 0
wcs.wcs.aux.dsun_obs = u.au.to(u.m)
wcs.wcs.dateobs = "2020-01-01T00:00:00"
wcs.wcs.dateavg = wcs.wcs.dateobs
wcs.fix()


ax = plt.subplot(111, projection=wcs)
plt.imshow(np.zeros((200, 200)))
ax.coords.grid(color='white')
ax.coords[0].set_axislabel("Custom frame X")
ax.coords[1].set_axislabel("Custom frame Y")

overlay = ax.get_coords_overlay('helioprojective')
overlay.grid(color='gold', ls='dotted')
overlay[0].set_axislabel("Helioprojective Tx")
overlay[1].set_axislabel("Helioprojective Ty")

This pull request fixes a bug in WCSAxes ticks/labels when overlaying a coordinate frame where a default unit is not degrees (hour angle, arcminutes, etc.).  The WCSAxes internal transformations work in degrees, but `coord_meta` was being loaded as if the internal transformations worked in the default unit.  The result was that the tick labels claim to be in the default units but have values in degree units.

The figure test in this PR overlays ICRS (top and right) on top of ICRS (bottom and left).  Before the fix in this PR:
![before](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/assets/991759/cfbc9215-1755-4498-8e7d-3a24f8db5eab)

After the fix in this PR:
![after](https://github.com/astropy/astropy/assets/991759/4dd733be-a8ca-491c-a103-3aa9e83336b2)
